## Welcome!

This is an R Markdown document in HTML format. It includes other syntax for authoring PDF and Word documents.\
For more details on using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>.

When you click the **Knit** button a document will be generated that includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code chunks within the document.

First, we're going to set up our code chunks.

## Set-up code chunk
```{r setup, include=T, message=F}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir="/Users/jackrodman/Documents/SCTC/practice data")


#This sets the working directory for the entire R Markdown file

#lets load some packages
library(ggplot2)
library(rstatix)
library(Hmisc)
library(jtools)
```

```{r loaddata, echo=T}
#we can now load data from the new working directory
places_data = read.csv("places_tf.csv", header=T, sep=",")

#lets subset the data to only save places with a better climate
climate_subset = subset(places_data, climate>=2.5)
summary(climate_subset$climate)

#how about a variable transformation
climate_subset$log_climate = log(climate_subset$climate)
str(climate_subset)
```
Both the new dataframe and the transformed variable will be stored in the .rmd file and can be readily used throughout the document

## General code structure
You can embed an R code chunk that shows both the results and the underlying code. Like this:

```{r embeded code}
summary(climate_subset)
```

Or you can generate output without showing the underlying R code:
```{r non-embedded code, echo=F}
summary(climate_subset$health)
summary(climate_subset$recreate)
```


## Including Plots

You can also embed plots within a report using either the base `plot()` function or `ggplot2` package, for example:

```{r ggplot, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.cap="This is a scatterplot",fig.align='center'}
ggplot(climate_subset, aes(x=recreate, y=health)) + geom_point(color="steelblue3") + 
      geom_smooth(method="lm", se=F) + theme_bw()

hist(climate_subset$health)
hist(climate_subset$recreate)
```


## Running Analyses
```{r correlation, echo=F}
#cor.test() function from the base stats package
cor.test(climate_subset$recreate, climate_subset$health, method="pearson", conf.level=0.95)
```
```{r multivariable linear regression, echo=T}
mod1 = lm(health ~ recreate + econ, data=climate_subset)
summ(mod1, confint=T, digits=2) #summ() function from the jtools package
```
Note that the `echo = TRUE` parameter was added to the code chunk to print the underlying R code. This also greatly helps with reproducibility as it allows others to see the methodlogy that was used to generate your results.


## Inline code
Inline code can also include functions or objects previously created in a regular code chunk. Inline code can show the underlying code without evaluating (aka just printing the code) or by evaluating and printing the code results. Like this!

Create an object that contains the mean climate in the 'places' dataset rounded to 3 digits
```{r}
mean_climate = round(mean(places_data$climate), digits=5)
```


**Then write new text that contains an inline code function with your created object**

The mean climate of all cars was `mean_climate`  -- only printing code\
The mean speed of all cars was `r mean_climate`  -- evaluating and printing results


This is new *text*

